sorular.soru: Can Teachable and WooCommerce work together?
sorular.cevap: Not through a first-party connector we could verify. Teachable's public site publishes no WooCommerce integration page, and searching the WooCommerce extension marketplace for "Teachable" returns no listed extension (both checked 10 September 2026). Teams bridge the two with Zapier, which publishes ready-made workflows in both directions — enrolling a user in a Teachable course when a WooCommerce order is placed, and creating a WooCommerce order from a new Teachable transaction. That means the link is real but it runs through a third service you also pay for and maintain.

sorular.soru: Which is cheaper for selling courses, Teachable or WooCommerce?
sorular.cevap: It depends on sales volume, because Teachable's entry plan charges a cut. Teachable Starter is $29/month billed annually plus a 7.5% transaction fee; Builder removes that fee at $69/month annually. So on $2,000 of monthly course sales, Starter's fee alone is $150 — more than the $40 gap to Builder, which is why the cheap plan stops being the cheap plan quickly. WooCommerce charges no platform fee at all: the core plugin is free and open source, but you carry hosting (typically $25–$350/month), paid extensions ($29–$299/year) and payment processing of roughly 2.5–2.9% + 30¢ through WooPayments. Both figures come from the vendors' own pricing pages.

Not with a connector GetResponse builds itself, as far as we can verify. GetResponse's own integration directory carries pages for JotForm, Gravity Forms, Paperform, Formstack, 123ContactForm and Contact Form 7 — but there is no Typeform page in it, and the expected URL returns a 404 (checked 10 September 2026). Two routes work in practice: Zapier, which publishes prebuilt actions such as creating or updating a GetResponse contact from a new Typeform entry, or a Typeform webhook posting into the GetResponse API if you would rather not add a third subscription.

sorular.soru: Are Typeform and GetResponse actually alternatives to each other?
sorular.cevap: Mostly no, and the pricing shows why. Typeform is priced on responses collected — free up to 100 responses a month, then $25/month annually for Basic at the same 100-response cap, $50 for 1,000 and $83 for 10,000. GetResponse is priced on what you do with contacts afterwards — Starter from $15.58/month annually with unlimited monthly email sends and one automation workflow, Marketer from $48.38 for unlimited automation. GetResponse does include its own signup forms, so it can replace a simple Typeform; it will not replace conditional logic-heavy forms. Most teams run both and pass data between them.

No. Drizzle's own Get started documentation lists its supported dialects as PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SingleStore, MSSQL, CockroachDB and Gel — every one of them a SQL engine (checked 10 September 2026). MongoDB is a document database and is not among them, and Drizzle's schema, query builder and migration tooling are all built around SQL tables. If you are on MongoDB, Mongoose or the official MongoDB driver is the equivalent layer; Drizzle only enters the picture if you move to a SQL engine.

They are not the same kind of purchase. Drizzle ORM itself is free and open source — the vendor publishes no price, and Drizzle Studio runs locally for free through drizzle-kit; only the hosted Gateway product is paid. MongoDB is the database you pay for: Atlas M0 is free at 512 MB with shared CPU and 100 operations per second, Flex runs $0.011/hour (about $8–$30/month) for 5 GB, and dedicated clusters start at M10 around $57/month, with egress billed separately.

sorular.soru: Which is cheaper for a team of 10, Linear or YouTrack?
sorular.cevap: YouTrack, and at that exact size it is free. YouTrack Cloud costs nothing for teams of up to 10 users, with no issue cap. Linear's Free plan is also $0 and allows unlimited members, but it stops at 2 teams and 250 issues — pass either limit and you are on Basic at $10 per user/month billed yearly, which is $100/month for those same 10 people. The eleventh user flips the comparison: YouTrack then charges $4.50 per user/month billed annually ($5.40 monthly), with the per-user rate falling as more seats are added.

sorular.soru: What is the real difference between the Linear and YouTrack free plans?
sorular.cevap: They cap opposite things. Linear caps the work: unlimited members, but 2 teams, 250 issues and 10 MB file uploads. YouTrack caps the people: up to 10 users, with issues and projects unbounded, plus a free helpdesk for 3 agents and unlimited reporters. So a small team with a long backlog outgrows Linear's free plan first, while a growing team with a short backlog outgrows YouTrack's first.

Stripe, on the headline rate — and the gap is wide. Stripe's standard rate is 2.9% + 30¢ per successful domestic card transaction with no setup or monthly fee; Paddle charges 5% + 50¢ per checkout transaction, also with no monthly fee. On $10,000 of monthly sales spread over 200 orders of $50, that works out to about $350 through Stripe against $600 through Paddle — roughly $250 a month more. The question is what the $250 buys, and for a lot of software companies it is not nothing: see below.

sorular.soru: What does Paddle's higher rate actually include?
sorular.cevap: Two things Stripe prices separately or leaves to you. First, tax: Paddle acts as merchant of record and its pricing page states that full sales-tax registration, filing and remittance are included — with Stripe, that registration and filing is your legal obligation, and Stripe Tax is a paid add-on. Second, disputes: Paddle publishes no additional charge for chargebacks, payouts or currency conversion, while Stripe charges $15.00 for each dispute received and another $15.00 for each dispute countered manually, refunded only if you win, plus 1.5% on international cards and 1% when a currency conversion is required. So a business selling globally with a moderate dispute rate closes much of the gap; a business selling domestically to low-risk customers does not, and should stay on Stripe. Both figures checked 10 September 2026.

kisaCevap.ozet: This is really Firebase Authentication versus Keycloak. Firebase Auth is a hosted service inside Google's app platform: email, phone and social sign-in with native SDKs for iOS, Android, web and Flutter, and nothing to run yourself; enterprise protocols such as SAML and OpenID Connect providers arrive through the paid Identity Platform tier. Keycloak is a self-hosted identity server from the Red Hat-backed open-source project: SAML 2.0 and OpenID Connect out of the box, LDAP and Active Directory user federation, realms for multi-tenancy, fine-grained roles and identity brokering to other providers. It ships no mobile SDK; apps talk to it through standard OIDC flows. The choice is operational: zero-ops managed auth for app teams versus full control and data ownership for platform teams.

firebase: you are already on Firebase or Google Cloud and want auth wired to Firestore rules in an afternoon
the product is mobile-first and you want first-party iOS, Android and Flutter SDKs
nobody on the team wants to run, patch or back up an identity server
keycloak: you need SAML, LDAP or Active Directory federation without a per-user cloud bill
users, sessions and tokens must stay on your own infrastructure
you run several tenants or brands and want realm-level isolation

kisaCevap.ozet: Slack is workplace messaging built around an organisation: channels, threads, search across everything and an app directory that plugs in Jira, GitHub, Google Drive and the rest, with paid plans unlocking message history, unlimited apps and SSO. Discord grew up around gaming communities: servers anyone can join, always-on voice channels, screen sharing and roles that scale to very large member counts, with the core product free. Discord is the better fit for public communities, open-source projects and companies that want a customer or developer community; Slack is the better fit for internal team communication where compliance, retention and integrations matter.

slack: internal company chat with retention, SSO and admin controls
deep integrations with your work tools and workflow automation
search across years of history is part of how the team works
discord: a public or semi-public community: users, players, open-source contributors
always-on voice rooms and screen sharing with no meeting to schedule
a large member base on a budget of zero

kisaCevap.ozet: Both are hosted storefronts, so neither needs a server. Shopify has the larger app store and theme market, the smoother checkout and point-of-sale story and its own payment processor; using a third-party gateway on Shopify adds a transaction fee on most plans. BigCommerce charges no extra transaction fee for outside gateways, ships more catalogue features natively (variants, faceted search, B2B price lists on higher tiers) and is friendlier to headless builds through its APIs. Small and mid-size brands usually pick Shopify for the ecosystem; larger catalogues, B2B sellers and teams committed to a specific payment provider lean BigCommerce.

shopify: you want the biggest app and theme ecosystem and the most third-party help
retail plus online with Shopify POS in the same account
you are happy to use Shopify Payments as your processor
bigcommerce: you must keep an existing payment gateway without an added platform fee
a large catalogue with complex variants or B2B price lists
a headless storefront on your own front end

kisaCevap.ozet: Teachable is a course platform first: curriculum builder, quizzes, certificates, coaching products and a student experience tuned for structured learning. Podia is a broader creator storefront: courses, digital downloads, webinars, memberships, email marketing and a website builder in one account, with a simpler course builder. If teaching is the product, Teachable's course tooling is deeper. If you sell a mix of downloads, community access and the occasional course, Podia bundles more of that under one roof.

teachable: structured courses with quizzes, completion certificates and drip schedules
coaching or cohort products alongside self-paced courses
you want the platform many students already recognise
podia: you sell downloads, memberships and webinars, not only courses
you want email marketing and a website in the same tool
a simpler builder is worth more to you than deep course features

kisaCevap.ozet: Trello is a kanban board: cards move across lists, and Power-Ups add calendars, timelines and automation. It is fast to learn and works for any team that thinks in boards. Teamwork.com is project management aimed at agencies and client-services teams: task lists, Gantt-style timelines, time tracking, billing and client permissions are built in. Trello is the lighter tool for tracking work; Teamwork is the one to pick when you bill clients for that work and need time, budgets and invoices in the same place.

trello: visual boards are how the team already thinks
a small team or personal workflow with light process
you want to start in minutes and grow through Power-Ups
teamwork: agency or client work with time tracking and billable hours
Gantt timelines, workload and budgets on every project
clients need their own login with restricted visibility

kisaCevap.ozet: WooCommerce is a free plugin that turns a WordPress site into a store; you own the hosting, the theme and every extension, and the plugin ecosystem is enormous. Ecwid by Lightspeed is a hosted cart you embed into any existing site, social profile or marketplace listing, with hosting, security and updates handled for you. WooCommerce gives control and no platform fee at the cost of maintenance; Ecwid gives a store that runs anywhere within the hour at the cost of flexibility.

woocommerce: you already run WordPress and want full control of theme and checkout
you need a specific extension only the WooCommerce ecosystem has
you would rather pay for hosting than a platform subscription
ecwid: your site is on Wix, Squarespace or a static builder and needs a cart
selling the same catalogue on the site, Instagram and marketplaces
nobody wants to maintain plugins and PHP updates

kisaCevap.ozet: Asana is a work-management tool organised around tasks, projects and goals, with list, board, timeline and calendar views and a strong mobile app. Smartsheet is a spreadsheet that learned project management: rows, columns and formulas at the core, with Gantt charts, dashboards, forms and enterprise reporting layered on top. Teams that already live in spreadsheets and need formulas, cross-sheet references and heavy reporting choose Smartsheet; teams that want a clean task tool with less setup choose Asana.

asana: cross-functional teams tracking tasks and goals, not cell formulas
you want an interface people adopt without training
workflow rules and forms matter more than reporting grids
smartsheet: your project plans are already spreadsheets with formulas
portfolio dashboards and roll-up reports across many projects
PMO-style resource management and enterprise controls

kisaCevap.ozet: Notion is a hosted workspace: pages, databases, shared docs, wikis and team permissions live in the cloud, with real-time collaboration and an API. Obsidian is a local-first note app: notes are plain Markdown files on your disk, linked into a graph and extended by community plugins, with sync and publishing as optional paid services. Notion is for teams that need one shared source of truth; Obsidian is for individuals who want ownership of their files, offline access and a personal knowledge graph.

notion: a team wiki, docs and databases everyone edits together
structured databases with relations, rollups and views
it should work the same in a browser on any machine
obsidian: your notes must be plain files you own and back up yourself
linked thinking, backlinks and a plugin ecosystem

kisaCevap.ozet: monday.com is a visual work OS: boards with status columns, automation recipes, dashboards and templates for marketing, CRM and development teams. Smartsheet keeps the spreadsheet as its core object and adds Gantt, dashboards, forms and enterprise governance. Both track projects; the difference is who sets them up. monday.com is built for teams that configure boards themselves and want an automation-heavy workflow; Smartsheet is built for planners and PMOs who need formulas, cross-sheet references and control over large portfolios.

monday: visual boards and automations set up by the team, not IT
marketing, sales pipeline and ops on one platform
onboarding speed and a friendly interface matter
smartsheet: formulas, cell linking and spreadsheet logic inside the plan
enterprise admin and governance across many workspaces

kisaCevap.ozet: ClickUp tries to be the one app for everything: tasks, docs, whiteboards, goals, chat and dashboards, with an unusually deep settings surface. Teamwork.com narrows the scope to client work: projects, time tracking, billing, workload and client access. If you want a single workspace to replace several tools and will invest in configuring it, ClickUp is the broader product. If you run an agency and the point is billing clients for tracked time, Teamwork has that flow built in without add-ons.

clickup: replacing docs, tasks and chat with one workspace
a team that enjoys customising views and automations
many small teams with different working styles on one account
teamwork: client-facing projects with billable hours and invoices
workload and capacity planning for a services team
a focused tool rather than a configurable platform

kisaCevap.ozet: Asana and Teamwork.com both manage tasks and projects, but they serve different rooms. Asana is the internal work tool: goals, portfolios, workflow rules and cross-team visibility, with a polished interface teams adopt quickly. Teamwork is the agency tool: time tracking, billing, budgets and client logins are core features rather than integrations. Pick Asana for coordinating work inside a company; pick Teamwork when the work is done for clients and has to be invoiced.

asana: internal projects and company goals across departments
a clean, widely known tool with minimal setup
reporting on progress matters more than tracking hours
teamwork: billable time, budgets and invoices per project
clients need controlled access to their own projects
resource and workload planning for a services team

kisaCevap.ozet: monday.com is a general work platform: boards, automations and dashboards you shape for sales, marketing, operations or development. Teamwork.com is project management for client-services teams, with time tracking, billing and client permissions in the box. monday.com wins on flexibility and breadth; Teamwork wins when your projects are billed to clients and the tool has to understand hours and budgets.

monday: several departments need one configurable platform
visual boards and automation recipes over process rigour
CRM, marketing and ops work sit alongside projects
teamwork: agency projects with billable hours and invoicing
clients log in to see their own projects
workload planning across a services team

kisaCevap.ozet: Claude is Anthropic's assistant, available as web and desktop apps, an API and the Claude Code agent for developers; it is known for long-document work, careful writing and coding. Gemini is Google's model family and assistant, woven into Search, Gmail, Docs, Android and Google Cloud, with strong multimodal input across text, image, audio and video. Choose by ecosystem and job: Claude for writing, analysis and agentic coding where the quality of reasoning is the point; Gemini when your work already lives in Google Workspace or you need native multimodal features and Google's cloud tooling.

claude: long documents, careful writing and code work
you build agents on the API and want strong tool use
you want a coding agent in the terminal or IDE
gemini: your team runs on Gmail, Docs and Drive and wants the assistant inside them
image, audio and video inputs are part of the workflow
you deploy on Google Cloud and Vertex AI

kisaCevap.ozet: Cloudflare is a network platform: CDN, DNS, DDoS protection, WAF, Zero Trust access, Workers for edge compute and R2 storage, with a free plan at the bottom and enterprise tiers above it. Bunny.net is a focused CDN and media company: pull and push zones, edge storage, image optimisation and video streaming, priced by traffic and known for simplicity and low cost. If you need security, DNS and edge apps in one place, Cloudflare is the platform. If you want a fast, inexpensive CDN for static assets, images or video with transparent pay-as-you-go pricing, Bunny.net is the specialist.

cloudflare: DNS, DDoS protection and a WAF in front of the whole site
edge functions and storage alongside caching
the free plan covers a small site
bunny-net: video delivery or large media libraries by the terabyte
predictable per-gigabyte pricing without plan tiers
a simple CDN in front of an existing origin

kisaCevap.ozet: These are different products that share the AI-media aisle. ElevenLabs makes voices: text-to-speech, voice cloning, dubbing and speech-to-text through an app and an API, and it is what developers embed when a product needs to speak. Synthesia makes videos: pick an AI avatar, paste a script and it produces a presenter-style training or marketing video with the voice included, aimed at learning and marketing teams rather than developers. If the deliverable is audio, or you are building a product, ElevenLabs. If the deliverable is a talking-head video without a camera, Synthesia.

elevenlabs: audio is the output: narration, dubbing, voice agents
you integrate speech into your own app through an API
synthesia: training, onboarding or explainer videos with an on-screen presenter
non-technical teams producing video from a script
templates and brand kits for corporate video

kisaCevap.ozet: Semrush is an SEO and content suite: keyword research, rank tracking, site audits, backlink analysis and PPC data, used to work on your own site's search performance. Similarweb is market intelligence: estimated traffic, traffic sources, audience overlap and app usage for any site, used to size markets and benchmark competitors. They overlap on competitor keywords but answer different questions. SEO teams doing the work choose Semrush; strategy, investment and sales teams who need to know how big a competitor is choose Similarweb.

semrush: day-to-day SEO: keywords, audits, rank tracking, backlinks
content planning and PPC research in one workspace
similarweb: traffic estimates and channel mix for sites you do not own
market sizing, benchmarking and competitive research
audience and app intelligence for strategy or sales prospecting

kisaCevap.ozet: Moz Pro is a classic SEO toolset: keyword research, rank tracking, site crawl and the Domain Authority link metric, priced for small teams and consultants. Similarweb is market and traffic intelligence: estimated visits, referral sources and audience data for any website or app. Moz helps you improve your own site's rankings; Similarweb tells you how much traffic a competitor gets and where it comes from. They are complements more than rivals.

moz: SEO fundamentals on a modest budget
link research and Domain Authority tracking
learning SEO with strong guides and community
similarweb: app and audience analytics beyond search

kisaCevap.ozet: Amplitude is product analytics: events, funnels, retention, cohorts and experimentation, built for product teams who instrument their app and ask quantitative questions. Hotjar is behaviour analytics: heatmaps, session recordings, surveys and feedback widgets that show what a user did on a page and why. Amplitude tells you where users drop off across the product; Hotjar shows you the screen where it happened. Many teams run both; if you only run one, product-led SaaS teams start with Amplitude and marketing or UX teams start with Hotjar.

amplitude: event-based funnels, retention and cohort analysis
a product team that instruments features and measures adoption
experiments and feature flags tied to analytics
hotjar: heatmaps and session replays of real visits
on-page surveys and feedback without engineering
conversion work on marketing and landing pages

kisaCevap.ozet: Airtable is a cloud database that looks like a spreadsheet: bases, views, forms, automations and interfaces, collaborative by default and quick to start. Claris FileMaker is a mature low-code platform for building custom business apps with its own scripting, layouts and relational engine, deployable on Claris Cloud or your own server and long used for internal systems that outlive the people who built them. Airtable is for teams who want a shared, flexible database today; FileMaker is for organisations building durable line-of-business apps with more control over logic, hosting and offline use.

airtable: a shared database the whole team edits in the browser
lightweight automations and interfaces without a developer
connecting to modern SaaS tools through integrations
filemaker: custom business apps with complex scripting and layouts
on-premise or private hosting and desktop clients
a long-lived internal system with a dedicated developer
